name: Chromium Oxide
notes: Toxic fumes, volatile at 2265 F (1241 C). Hazardous. Powerful green color, may require ball milling.

name: Cobalt Oxide
notes: Black cobalt oxide, Co₃O₄, often sold as "71% cobalt". In a glaze it counts as CoO: 93.4% CoO with 6.6% loss on ignition. Gives up oxygen to become CoO at about 900–950 C (1650–1740 F) in air, lower in reduction. About 1.5 times as strong as cobalt carbonate (1.48 by CoO content; carbonate grades vary). Strong blue at 0.25 percent. Toxic: a skin and respiratory sensitizer, and cobalt compounds are suspected carcinogens when breathed in; avoid the dust.

name: Cobalt carbonate
notes: Sold as a basic carbonate with variable cobalt (about 45–47% Co). Counted here as CoO, about 63% CoO with 37% loss on ignition; decomposes to CoO in the firing. Insoluble in water. Use about 1.5 times the weight of cobalt oxide. Toxic: classified as a carcinogen by inhalation and a skin and respiratory sensitizer; avoid the dust.

name: Copper oxide
notes: Black copper oxide, CuO. Melts at about 1326 C (2419 F), but in air first loses oxygen to Cu₂O from about 1010–1030 C (1850–1890 F). Strong, active flux; can make glazes run. Copper becomes increasingly volatile above about 1025 C (1877 F) and can flash onto nearby ware, especially tin whites. Coarser than the carbonate, so it can speckle. Over about 5% can give black metallic surfaces unsuitable for food ware. Harmful if swallowed; vent the kiln.

name: Copper carbonate
notes: Basic copper carbonate, CuCO₃•Cu(OH)₂, sold as "copper carbonate": a green powder (typically 200 mesh). Does not melt: decomposes to CuO from about 290 C (554 F), giving off water and CO₂. Counted here as CuO, about 64% CuO with 36% loss on ignition. Gives more even color than black copper oxide. Active flux. Fumes from about 815 C (1500 F) and can flash onto nearby ware, especially tin whites. Harmful if swallowed.

name: Ilmenite
notes: A natural source of iron and titanium in glazes.

name: Iron oxide
relatedTo: Black iron oxide, yellow iron oxide, magnetic iron
notes: Red iron oxide, Fe₂O₃. Stabilizing refractory in oxidation firing until cone 7 - 8. Thermally decomposes to FeO at cone 7 - 8, becomes a strong flux. In reduction will reduce to black iron oxide early in firing and likewise is a strong flux.

name: Black iron oxide
relatedTo: Magnetite, magnetic iron oxide, red iron oxide
notes: Magnetite, Fe₃O₄, also sold as magnetic iron oxide; some grades are ground natural ore containing quartz. Older potters’ books list black iron as FeO, but ferrous oxide is not sold as a potter’s material. Gram for gram it gives about as much iron as red iron oxide. A strong flux in reduction. Often coarser than red iron oxide; sieve or ball-mill it to avoid specks.

name: Yellow iron oxide
relatedTo: Red iron oxide, black iron oxide
notes: A hydrated form of iron oxide. Insoluble in water, very fine particles.

name: Yellow ochre
notes: A material with hydrated iron oxide and clay. Sometimes called limonite (as a mineral of iron oxide). Many also have manganese.

name: Manganese dioxide
notes: MnO₂. Loses oxygen in stages as it heats: to Mn₂O₃ at about 450–600 C (840–1110 F), then to Mn₃O₄ at about 750–1100 C (1380–2010 F); the gas can cause bubbles. In a glaze it counts as MnO (81.6% MnO, 18.4% loss on ignition); grades of ground ore may be only about 75% MnO₂. A flux once dissolved in the melt; undissolved particles stiffen low-fired glazes. Harmful if swallowed or breathed in; manganese fumes at high temperatures, so vent the kiln.

name: Nickel oxide, green
notes: Toxic: classified as a carcinogen by inhalation. Volatile at high temperatures, creating toxic fumes. Unstable above 2192 F (1200 C).

name: Nickel oxide, black
notes: Toxic: classified as a carcinogen by inhalation. Volatile at high temperatures, creating toxic fumes. Unstable above 2192 F (1200 C).

name: Praseodymium Oxide
notes: Pr₆O₁₁, the form usually sold: a dark brown powder. Does not melt in a kiln (it melts at about 2183 C / 3961 F); the 931 C often quoted is for the metal. Loses a little oxygen when heated but stays a mixed oxide in air. Low toxicity on current classifications (at most an eye, skin and respiratory irritant); rare-earth oxides can carry traces of thorium. Usually used in zircon-praseodymium yellow stains; as a raw oxide it gives pale lime to yellow greens at about 5–8%.

name: Rutile
notes: Titanium dioxide with some iron: here 0.05 Fe₂O₃ to each TiO₂, about 9% iron oxide by weight. Dark and light rutile sources are available, which will have varied properties in terms of ratios of iron and titanium.

name: Titanium dioxide
notes: TiO₂. Added at about 2–10% (4% is typical) for variegation, opacity and crystal growth, and with iron or cobalt for broken colors. Also in the materials list as Titanium Oxide, for recipes that count it in the base.

name: Vanadium oxide
notes: Toxic fumes. Melts at 1274 F (690 C), and volatile at higher temperatures. Very strong flux.

name: Tin oxide
notes: Stannic oxide, SnO₂. Insoluble. Does not melt at glaze temperatures (it melts at about 1630 C / 2966 F); it stays suspended as fine particles, which is what makes the glaze opaque. 4–7% gives a soft white, 8–10% full opacity, and a warm white in low-fired majolica. Opacifies poorly in reduction (it forms SnO) and at cone 10, where it starts to dissolve. Helps develop copper reds in reduction; with a trace of chrome it gives pinks. Low toxicity; breathing the dust over years can cause stannosis, a benign lung condition.

name: Zirconium oxide
notes: Zirconium dioxide, ZrO₂ (zirconia). Rarely used raw in glazes: most recipes call for zircon (Zircopax, Superpax), which is zirconium silicate. Insoluble; opacifies as it stays unmelted at glaze temperatures, stiffens the melt and can reduce crazing.

name: Zircon
relatedTo: Zirconium silicate, Zircopax, Superpax, Excelopax, Ultrox, Zircosil, zirconium oxide
notes: Zirconium silicate, ZrSiO₄: 67.2% ZrO₂ and 32.8% SiO₂. Sold as Zircopax, Superpax, Excelopax, Ultrox and Zircosil, which differ mainly in particle size. The usual opacifier: about 4–7% for semi-opaque, 8–15% or more for full opacity; 1–3% mainly hardens the glaze. Works in reduction, unlike tin oxide. Its silica counts toward the glaze.
